title: International finance, part 1: interest rate parity - why a forward rate is not a forecast
subtitle: The interest rate gap sets the forward points, and why a high rate does not mean a profit
whyItMatters: A great many people believe that parking money in the high-interest currency and hedging the exchange rate is a way to earn a risk-free profit. Interest rate parity proves that no such thing exists, and understanding why will change how you read every forward quote you ever see.
openingQuestion: What mainly determines the forward exchange rate?
openingOptions: The bank's own forecast of where the rate is heading soon
The interest rate gap between the two currencies at that tenor
The trade balance between the two countries in the latest period
The intervention the central bank plans over that tenor
explanation: A forward rate is the output of a no-arbitrage calculation, not a prediction. If you could borrow the low-interest currency, swap into the high-interest one, put it on deposit and at the same time lock in the rate at which you sell it back through a forward contract, you would earn a risk-free profit whenever the forward rate failed to adjust. The market closes that gap instantly by pushing the forward points to exactly the interest rate differential. This is the same replication argument you met in the derivatives stage, applied to currencies.

diagram.label: Swap and deposit in the high-interest currency
Lock the sell-back rate with a forward contract
Profit is zero - that is interest rate parity

realWorldExample.company: A company borrowing in foreign currency because the rate is low
realWorldExample.description: A Vietnamese company sees that dollar borrowing costs far less than dong borrowing and decides to fund in dollars a project that only generates dong revenue. The rate differential they take to be a saving is in fact compensation for the currency risk they have just absorbed. If they buy a forward contract to strip that risk out, the cost of the forward will eat almost the whole rate differential - exactly as interest rate parity predicts.

quiz.question: What does covered interest rate parity state?
options: The two countries' interest rates converge in the long run
The hedged return on the two currencies must be equal
Spot always equals the forward rate at every quoted tenor
The central bank must move rates to track the exchange rate
quiz.explanation: Once the exchange rate is locked in through a forward contract, the two investments become equally risk-free, so they must deliver the same return. This is a relationship enforced by real arbitrage rather than a hypothesis waiting to be tested. Rates in two countries do not converge - they can stay far apart indefinitely, and the forward points simply absorb the difference. Spot equalling forward would in fact be the violation, since it would leave the differential unpriced, and nothing here obliges a central bank to chase the exchange rate with policy.

quiz.question: How is the higher-interest currency quoted in the forward market?
options: Unchanged - rates do not touch the forward FX market at all
At a forward premium to the current spot rate
At a forward discount to the current spot rate
It depends on expected inflation differences between the two
quiz.explanation: This is the counter-intuitive part. A higher interest rate has to be paired with expected depreciation inside the forward quote, otherwise arbitrage would be available, which is why the high-yielding currency always trades at a discount in a forward contract. Quoting it at a premium would hand the arbitrageur both the interest and the currency gain. Interest rates are precisely what drives the forward market, and while inflation matters for the long-run spot path, covered parity is settled by nominal rates alone.

quiz.question: How does an unhedged currency carry trade work?
options: Invest in the government bonds of the highest-rated sovereign
Borrow and invest within one currency to harvest the maturity spread
Buy forwards at two banks to pocket the quote difference
Borrow the low-rate currency, invest the high-rate one, unhedged
quiz.explanation: Drop the hedge and the interest differential turns into a potential profit, in exchange for taking on the whole currency risk. It is the strategy famous for earning steadily for years and then losing enormously over a handful of days when the funding currency suddenly appreciates. Buying a top-rated sovereign bond is a credit decision, not a carry trade, borrowing and lending within one currency is a maturity play, and arbitraging two banks' forward quotes is a dealing-desk activity that involves no interest differential at all.

quiz.question: Why should a company not borrow in foreign currency purely because the nominal rate is lower?
options: Because the rate gap is the price of the FX risk just taken on
Because the foreign rate steps up by contract after year one
Because rules cap how much local firms may borrow abroad
Because bank conversion fees exceed the interest saved
quiz.explanation: Borrowing in foreign currency while earning revenue in the local one creates a currency mismatch between assets and liabilities - the same class of risk as the maturity mismatch covered in the corporate bond lesson. The interest saving is only an advance on a currency loss that may arrive later. There is no contractual step-up built into a foreign-currency loan, regulation is not what makes the trade unwise, and conversion fees are far too small to account for a differential of several percentage points.

quiz.question: Why is borrowing cheap foreign currency not inherently cheaper than borrowing expensive local currency?
options: Because the foreign borrowing rate ratchets up over the life of the loan
Because the rate gap is usually offset by the local currency's slide
Because the firm pays a conversion fee on every repayment instalment
Because banks demand more collateral against foreign-currency loans
quiz.explanation: Interest rate parity says the gain from the lower rate is in theory cancelled out by the currency move. A company with no foreign-currency revenue that borrows abroad because the rate looks cheap is really placing a bet on the exchange rate rather than saving on the cost of capital. The rate itself does not ratchet up by contract, conversion charges are a rounding error next to the differential, and collateral requirements are a lending condition, not the reason the apparent saving disappears.

keyTakeaways: A forward rate is the output of a no-arbitrage argument, not a bank's forecast
The higher-interest currency always trades at a discount in a forward quote
The interest differential after hedging is zero - there is no free lunch here
Borrowing in foreign currency because the rate is low is taking on currency risk, not saving on the cost of capital

practicePrompt.question: Currency A pays 8% and currency B pays 2%, one-year tenor. How will a forward contract price currency A?
options: A premium of about 6% over the current spot rate
A discount of about 6% against the current spot rate
Unchanged, since rates play no part in setting forwards
Undetermined without the inflation gap between the two
practicePrompt.explanation: If it did not depreciate by exactly the interest differential, anyone could borrow currency B, deposit in currency A and lock the exchange rate for a risk-free profit. Note that this says nothing about where spot will actually be in a year - it only says what price you can lock in today.

summary.keyIdea: Forward points are the interest rate differential, not a view about the future
summary.formula: Forward rate ≈ Spot rate × (1 + quote currency rate) / (1 + base currency rate)
summary.commonMistake: Reading the forward rate as the market's forecast and then trading on it
summary.action: Take a one-year forward quote for a currency pair and check whether it lines up with the interest rate differential.

application.title: Test every proposal to borrow in foreign currency
application.message: Ask exactly one question: which currency does this project's revenue come in? If it differs from the borrowing currency, the interest saved is the risk premium, and you need to quantify it through the cost of hedging rather than ignore it.
application.secondary: The founding principle of currency risk management: try to match the currency of the debt to the currency of the cash flow.

sections.text: There is a question that sounds naive but opens up the whole of international finance: if this currency pays 8% and that one only pays 2%, why doesn't everyone pile into the first? The answer is the mechanism that keeps the world free of free money, and it determines every forward quote you will ever see.

example.title: Why there can be no exception
example.calculation: If F sits above the formula: borrow the base currency, deposit the quote currency, sell forward
example.result: A risk-free profit requiring no capital
example.explanation: The moment the gap is wide enough to cover transaction costs, FX trading desks will do this in enormous size, and that action alone drags F back to the formula within seconds.

left.label: Hedged
left.text: Lock the exchange rate with a forward contract. The returns on both sides are equal. No risk left, and no extra profit left either.

right.label: Unhedged
right.text: Keep the currency risk in order to earn the interest differential. Steady gains over a long stretch, then very fast losses when the funding currency appreciates.

sections.label: The easiest thing to get wrong
sections.text: A forward rate does not tell you where the exchange rate will be. It only tells you the price you can lock in today. Empirically, the forward rate is a rather poor forecasting tool - and that very gap is where the currency carry trade earns its return, along with the tail risk that comes with it.

lines: Interest rate parity constrains today's price; it says nothing about tomorrow.
The next lesson covers the relationship that constrains exchange rates over the long run: purchasing power parity.
